claims.text: A conventional, temperable low-alloy martensitic steel can be made to exhibit a ductile-brittle-ductile transition.
Optimized thermal and thermomechanical treatments can induce this transition.
Impurity segregation causes temper embrittlement within a narrow temperature window.
The proposed low-alloy steel initially exhibits overall ductile behavior.
Tuning tempering temperature, hold time, and cooling rate can promote controlled impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
Phosphorus is an example of an impurity that may segregate to grain boundaries in the proposed steel.
The material is ductile at lower temperatures, brittle in an intermediate narrow temperature window, and ductile again at higher temperatures.
Segregation of impurities such as phosphorus to grain boundaries during tempering drives embrittlement.
Heat-treatment parameters control impurity diffusion and segregation.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation locally weakens grain boundaries.
Local grain-boundary weakening sharply decreases ductility within a narrow temperature interval.
Below and above the embrittlement window, impurity effects are minimized or reversed, restoring ductility.
Untreated or conventionally processed tempered martensitic steel maintains relatively consistent ductility without a pronounced embrittlement window.
The proposed behavior is limited to conventional, low-complexity alloys that permit impurity segregation.
Impurity segregation is inhibited in high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
High-entropy or compositionally complex alloys will not exhibit the proposed ductile-brittle-ductile behavior.
The temperature range and magnitude of the ductility drop depend on impurity concentration and heat-treatment parameters.
